strengths: The combination of graph neural networks with a language model based on ECFP is novel.
The method outperforms other baseline methods include MolCLR.
The paper addresses an important problem in molecular representation, which is a timely and relevant area of research.

The idea of using ECFP hashes as tokens for language modelling is an elegant solution to the problems with SMILES-based language models and introduces a much needed chemical inductive bias to the modelling paradigm. The comparison between ECFP-BERT and ChemBERTa seem to support this conclusion with the former outperforming the latter in 8 out of 11 datasets.

The idea of only masking atom and edge types during pretraining of the graph models makes a lot of intuitive sense and is an interesting incremental contribution to previous efforts (lines 427-431 and Figure 6).
The insight as to what GNN architecture might be a better choice depending on the dataset size is also an interesting finding (lines 481-485).
The paper is written clearly and concisely, main claims and contributions are succinctly expressed. The analysis and discussion are well written.
weaknesses: The main problem of the paper is about the baseline selection. The authors cited the "Dual-view Molecular Pre-training" (DVMP) paper but didn't use it as a baseline, and the paper should have used the DVMP method as a baseline to prove the necessity of using ECFP over SMILES for a language model.

Lack of sequential information: ECFP fingerprints are unordered sets while language models like RoBERTa assume ordered token sequences, causing a mismatch and potentially ignoring important chemical graph structure.
Use of BPE tokenization on ECFP hashes leads to loss of critical information because breaking compact hash representations yields uninformative tokens.
Masked token prediction as a self‑supervised task is less intuitive for ECFP tokens since there is no inherent relationship between neighboring ECFP hashes.

The contrastive learning approach for the GNN model may be ineffective because different molecules have varying graph structures, leading to naturally greater distances between positive‑negative pairs, and the paper lacks a clear description of the graph augmentation methods.
The authors do not provide information on how they split the data in the MoleculeNet dataset, raising concerns about the comparability and reliability of the reported results.

There is an important methodological inconsistency regarding the nature of the pre‑training dataset: the methods section states training on ECFPs derived from PubChem and ZINC, but the experiments section mentions only a 10‑million entry PubChem dataset.

The baselines in Tables 1 and 2 are insufficient; the only alternative LM considered is an outdated ChemBERTa, missing newer models like ChemBERTa‑2 and MolFormer‑XL, and lacking traditional ML baselines (MLP, SVM, Random Forest, etc.) to demonstrate the benefit of ECFP‑BERT.
Table values should be accompanied by measures of error across different runs to assess stability and statistical significance of differences between models.

An ablation study is needed to evaluate the performance of the pre‑trained GCN, GIN, and Graphformer architectures alone without BERT, and to compare with a transformer trained on SMILES to properly demonstrate the superior performance of the presented approach.
